passages.happening:
Jesus turns from how to treat others to how to live before God. He begins with a warning: “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them” (verse 1). If you do, you have no reward from your Father in heaven.

The first example is giving to the poor. Do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and streets, to be praised by people. They already have their full reward. Instead, “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (verse 3). Give in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 is about three practices that every devout Jew knew: giving to the poor, prayer and fasting. Jesus does not say ‘if you give’, ‘if you pray’ and ‘if you fast’. He says ‘when’. He takes it for granted that his followers will do all three. His question is who they do them for.

‘Hypocrite’ comes from the ordinary Greek word for a stage actor, someone playing a part. Matthew uses the word far more than the other Gospels. The picture is religion as a show, with an audience and applause.

No ancient writer describes givers really blowing trumpets. Most readers take it as a picture, like our saying ‘blowing your own trumpet’. And the left hand not knowing what the right hand does is a picture too. Give so quietly that you hardly notice yourself.
passages.ot: Think of the last good thing you did that nobody knew about. How did it feel to leave it unseen? Ask whose applause you are most hungry for, and whether you could give something this week that no one but God will ever know about.
passages.asks:
Is it wrong for anyone to know that you give? Not in itself. In chapter 5 Jesus told his followers to let people see their good deeds so that they give glory to God (5:16). The early church gave in plain sight (Acts 4:36-37). The problem is giving in order to be praised. Some churches and charities rightly keep public records of gifts for honesty's sake. The question Jesus presses is the motive in the heart, which only the giver and God can see.

What about ‘reward’? Jesus is not offering a payment for good deeds. He is saying that the Father notices what no one else sees, and that his ‘well done’ is worth more than the crowd's.

passages.happening:
The second example is prayer. Do not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen. They already have their reward. Instead, “go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen” (verse 6).

And do not babble on like the pagans, who think they will be heard because of their many words. Do not be like them, “for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Devout Jews kept set hours of prayer; Acts speaks of “the hour of prayer” (Acts 3:1). People often prayed standing; Jesus says, “when you stand to pray” (Mark 11:25). A man caught in a busy street at the hour of prayer would be seen by everyone. Jesus is not attacking public prayer as such. He is warning against arranging to be seen.

The ‘inner room’ was a storeroom or inner chamber, a private place with a door that shut.

‘Pagans’ means people who worshiped other gods. Jesus describes prayer that hopes to be heard because of its many words, as if a god had to be worn down. Jesus says the Father is not like that. He does not need to be persuaded to listen. He already knows.
passages.ot:
If the Father already knows what we need, why pray at all? Christians have answered that prayer is not giving God information. It is speaking with a Father, the way a child asks a parent who already knows. Jesus himself prayed often, and in the next verses he teaches his followers what to say. Many have found that prayer changes the one who prays as much as anything else.

Does this rule out long prayers or prayers said together? No. Jesus prayed all night (Luke 6:12). What he warns against is many words used as a tool to get God's attention, or to impress other people.
passages.hard: Where is your ‘inner room’, the place you can shut the door and speak to God with no one watching? If you do not have one, could you find one? And if you find prayer hard because you do not know the right words, take heart. Jesus says the Father is not waiting for the right words.
passages.asks: The prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel called on their god “from morning until noon,” and there was no answer (1 Kings 18:26). The Teacher in Ecclesiastes says, “God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few” (Ecclesiastes 5:2).

passages.happening:
Now Jesus gives his followers a prayer. “So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name’” (verse 9). Then come six requests. That God's kingdom would come and his will be done on earth as in heaven. That he would give us our daily bread. That he would forgive our debts as we have forgiven our debtors. That he would not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.

Then Jesus adds a word about forgiveness. If you forgive others, your Father will forgive you. If you do not, neither will he.
passages.hearers:
‘Hallowed’ means treated as holy. The first three requests are about God: his name, his kingdom, his will. Only then come our needs: bread, forgiveness, protection.

Calling God ‘Father’ was not new in Israel: “You, O LORD, are our Father” (Isaiah 63:16). But Jesus makes it the center. His followers may speak to God the way he does. A Jewish prayer called the Kaddish, still said in synagogues, also asks God to establish his kingdom in the lifetime of those who pray. How old its wording is, and how close to Jesus' day, is not known.

The word translated ‘daily’ is a puzzle. It is very rare in Greek. The early Christian scholar Origen (in the 200s) said he could find it in no other Greek writer and thought the Gospel writers had formed it. It may mean ‘for today’, ‘for tomorrow’, or ‘what we need to live’. Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, even rendered it ‘supersubstantial’ in Matthew, and some read it as pointing to the bread of the Lord's Supper as well. Whatever the exact sense, the prayer asks for enough, one day at a time.

Luke's version says “forgive us our sins” (Luke 11:4). So ‘debts’ here means sins, what we owe God and others.

The word for ‘temptation’ also means ‘test’ or ‘trial’. ‘Lead us not into temptation’ is a plea not to be brought into a trial too hard to bear. The New Testament is clear that God “cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (James 1:13). In 2017 Pope Francis said the usual wording was not a good translation, because it could sound as if God pushes us into sin, and the wording used in some languages has since been changed. Others keep the old words and read them as this humble plea.
passages.ot:
Does verse 15 mean we earn God's forgiveness by forgiving others? Most Christian traditions say no. In Jesus' parable in chapter 18, the king cancels the servant's huge debt first and freely. The servant is condemned because he refuses to pass on the mercy he received (18:33). Forgiving others is the sign that God's forgiveness has really reached us, not the price of it. A heart that holds on to every debt has not let God's mercy in.

Forgiveness has also been misused. Some have told people who were abused to forgive quickly, keep quiet, or go back to the person who hurt them. That is not what this prayer asks. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported. A person can forgive and still stay safe, still tell the truth, and still ask for justice. It can also take a long time, and that is not failure.
passages.hard: Pray the prayer slowly, one line at a time, and notice where you stop. Is it at ‘Your will be done’? At ‘as we also have forgiven’? That may be where God is at work in you. And notice that every request is ‘us’ and ‘our’. No one prays this prayer alone.
passages.asks:
Israel in the wilderness gathered manna each morning, “enough for that day” (Exodus 16:4). A wise man in Proverbs prays, “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion” (Proverbs 30:8).

Many Bibles add a closing line in a footnote: ‘For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.’ It is not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew, such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and early writers who explained the prayer do not include it. A short form, ‘Yours is the power and the glory forever’, appears in the Didache, an early Christian handbook from around AD 100, which also tells believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. Most scholars think the line was added early, as the church prayed the prayer aloud in worship. Its words echo David's prayer: “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory” (1 Chronicles 29:11). Christians who say it are praying good and biblical words, whether or not Matthew wrote them.

passages.happening: The third example is fasting. When you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, who make their faces unsightly so that people will see they are fasting. They have their reward. Instead, “anoint your head and wash your face” (verse 17), so that only your Father, who sees in secret, knows. And he will reward you.
passages.hearers:
Fasting means going without food, or some foods, for a time, to seek God. The Law of Moses required it only on the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to ‘humble yourselves’ (Leviticus 16:29). But devout people fasted more often. In Luke, a Pharisee says, “I fast twice a week” (Luke 18:12).

In Israel, people in grief or distress might go without washing or oiling their hair, or put ashes on their heads (2 Samuel 14:2; 13:19). When David's mourning ended, he “washed and anointed himself” (2 Samuel 12:20). Washing and oil meant an ordinary day. So Jesus says: look like you always do. Let the fast be between you and God.

Again Jesus says ‘when you fast’, not ‘if’. His followers did fast after he was gone (9:15; Acts 13:2-3).
passages.ot: A word of care. Fasting is not for everyone. People who are ill, pregnant, nursing, taking medicine that needs food, or who have a history of disordered eating should not go without food. No one should fast in a way that harms the body. Ask a doctor first, and if not eating has become a struggle for you, please talk to someone you trust and a health professional. There are other ways to set something aside to seek God, such as time on a screen or a small comfort.
passages.hard: Is there something you could set aside for a while, quietly, to make room for God? The point is not to prove anything. It is to want God more than the thing you gave up. And if you do give something up, do not tell anyone. See what it is like to keep it between you and the Father.
passages.asks: The prophets had already warned against fasting for show. “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). Isaiah says the fast God wants is “to share your bread with the hungry” and “to set the oppressed free” (Isaiah 58:6-7).

passages.t: Treasure, the eye, and two masters
passages.happening:
Do not store up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. Store up treasures in heaven, where none of that can happen. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (verse 21).

The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eye is good, your whole body will be full of light. If it is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness.

“No one can serve two masters.” Sooner or later you will love one and despise the other. “You cannot serve both God and money” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Wealth in Jesus' world was often kept as grain in a barn, as fine clothes and cloth, or as coins hidden in the house or buried in the ground (25:18). Moths could ruin cloth. Rust and decay could eat away at metal and stores. And thieves could break in. Nothing stored was really safe.

The ‘good eye’ and ‘bad eye’ come from a Hebrew way of speaking. A ‘good eye’ meant a generous spirit. Proverbs 22:9, “A generous man will be blessed,” literally says ‘good of eye’. An ‘evil eye’ meant a stingy, grudging one. Deuteronomy 15:9 warns against looking at a poor brother ‘begrudgingly’, literally with an evil eye. So Jesus may be saying that a generous heart fills a life with light, and a grasping one fills it with darkness. Some readers take the saying more broadly, about seeing clearly and with single focus. Both fit the passage.

The word translated ‘money’ is the Aramaic word mammon, which meant wealth or property. It was not the name of a god. But Jesus speaks of it as a master who wants your service.
passages.ot: Is Jesus against owning anything, or against saving for the future? Christians have read him differently. Some, like the monks and nuns of many centuries, have given up all property. Most have read the passage as being about where the heart rests, not a ban on owning or saving. Paul tells those who are rich not to put their hope in wealth but in God, and “to be generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17-18). What no reading allows is the claim that following God is a way to get rich. Jesus says the opposite. Money is a master that wants your heart, and you cannot give your heart to two.
passages.hard: Look at where your money and your time went last month. Jesus says that will tell you where your heart is. Is there anything you are holding so tightly that it has started to hold you? What would it look like to loosen your grip by giving some of it away?
passages.asks: Jesus' warning echoes the wisdom of Proverbs, which says that riches fly away like an eagle (Proverbs 23:5). Paul later writes that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10).

passages.happening:
“Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear” (verse 25). Look at the birds. They do not sow or reap or store food in barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more? Who can add a single hour to his life by worrying?

Consider the lilies of the field. They do not work or spin, yet not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of them. If God clothes the grass, which is here today and burned tomorrow, will he not clothe you, you of little faith?

So do not worry. The nations chase after these things, and your Father knows you need them. “But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you” (verse 33). Do not worry about tomorrow. “Today has enough trouble of its own” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Jesus' examples come from village work. Sowing, reaping and storing grain were the work of the fields. Spinning thread and making cloth were the work of the home. The birds and the flowers do neither, and yet they are fed and clothed.

The ‘lilies of the field’ were probably wildflowers. No one can say for sure which flower Jesus meant. Solomon's riches were famous; 1 Kings 10 describes his gold, his throne and his court.

‘O you of little faith’ is a gentle rebuke in Matthew, spoken to followers, not enemies. It means trusting God, but not enough to stop being afraid. Jesus says it again to the disciples in the storm (8:26) and to Peter sinking in the water (14:31), and both times he helps them.

The Greek for ‘worry’ can also mean ordinary care. Paul uses it for proper concern for others (Philippians 2:20). What Jesus warns against is the anxious grasping that makes food and clothes into masters, as in verse 24.
passages.ot:
Is Jesus saying that anxiety is a sin? This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Jesus himself was “sorrowful and deeply distressed” in the garden (26:37). The New Testament's answer to anxiety is an invitation, not an accusation. Getting help is not a lack of faith. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay. If you have reached the place where you are not sure you want to be here at all, tell someone today, and in the United States you can call or text 988 right now.

A skeptic can fairly say that birds do starve and believers do go hungry. Jesus does not promise otherwise. In chapter 10 he says sparrows fall, though not apart from the Father (10:29). Paul knew hunger (2 Corinthians 11:27). The promise is that the Father knows and cares, and Jesus makes his followers responsible for feeding the hungry (25:35). Nor is this a promise of wealth. ‘All these things’ are food and clothes, the needs of one day.
passages.hard: What are you most worried about right now? Name it. Then ask what one step of seeking God's kingdom today would look like, and leave tomorrow for tomorrow. If worry has become more than you can carry, that is not a failure of faith. Tell someone, and let them help.
passages.asks: God “provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call” (Psalm 147:9). Peter later echoes Jesus: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).
